newsitem.title: USA: White House resists subpoenas in Espy case.
newsitem.headline: White House resists subpoenas in Espy case.

text.p: The Clinton administration has refused to turn over documents sought by a grand jury investigating former Agriculture Secretary Mike Espy for allegedly accepting gifts and favors from companies he regulated, sources close to the case said Thursday.
The secret proceeding linked to subpoenas issued in 1994 and 1995 is now pending before a federal appeals court, the sources said.
"We're not commenting at all on the Espy grand jury investigation," said a White House spokesman.

The appeal of the subpoenas is under seal as part of a grand jury proceeding looking into allegations that Espy accepted illegal gifts from comopanies his agency regulated. He has said he did nothing wrong while serving as Clinton's first agriculture secretary until resigning in 1994.
Federal court rules require grand jury matters to remain secret, along with any challenges of subpoenas.

A decision by the appeals court on the two subpoenas could be appealed to the U.S. Supreme Court, much like the action by the White House earlier this week in the long-running Whitewater investigation.

The sources said the Clinton administration has refused to comply with a 1994 subpoena requesting certain materials and documents from the White House's own ethics review of Espy. The White House also balked at a 1995 subpoena that asked for documents about political appointments at Espy's former agency, the sources said.

On Thursday Barbara Pryor, the wife of former Arkansas Sen. David Pryor, testified before the Washington grand jury investigating Espy, the sources said. The panel meets on Tuesdays and Thursdays at the federal courthouse.
"We can't and don't comment about testimony before the grand jury," said Charles Blakly, a spokesman for independent counsel Donald Smaltz.

The grand jury probe of Espy has returned a series of indictments or convictions against more than a dozen individuals and concerns. Last month Espy's former chief of staff pleaded innocent to criminal charges of hiding some $22,000 in fees he received from farm groups while working for Espy.

Tuesday, Sun-Diamond Growers of California was fined $1.5 million by a federal court for giving illegal gifts to Espy. A senior company executive, Richard Douglas, was separately indicted for allegedly giving Espy a lavish weekend outing at the U.S. Tennis Open Tournament in 1993 and other gifts.
Sun-Diamond, a cooperative owned by fruit producers, sold products to the Agriculture Department for use in school lunch programs.

The investigation of Espy has proceeded quietly during the past 30 months, overshadowed by a separate probe led by independent counsel Kenneth Starr into the Clintons' connections to a failed Arkansas savings and loan and the Whitewater real estate venture.
